title: Three perfect days in Paris, in the year photography turns 200
dek: The Marais on Friday, Rodin, Monet and a free night of photographs on Saturday, and the Canal Saint-Martin on Sunday, in the quiet week before Paris Photo.

hero.caption: Place des Vosges, the Marais square where Friday begins.

intro:
France is marking two hundred years since Nicéphore Niépce fixed the first lasting photograph in 1826, and this is the weekend Paris turns that into exhibitions. The Louvre opened *Louvre Photo* on November 4: more than 300 pictures of the palace itself, its galleries, visitors and staff. At the Bourse de Commerce, *Remember Me* fills the building with about 700 photographs from the Pinault Collection, and on Saturday evening it is free. Across the river, PhotoSaintGermain has spread more than thirty free shows through Left Bank galleries, bookshops and schools since Thursday. Paris Photo itself does not open at the Grand Palais until November 12, so this is the calmer week to see photographs before the crowds arrive.

The rest of the plan stays close to the ground. Friday is the Marais, with a free history museum, Picasso's house and dinner at a Provençal bistro. Saturday crosses from Rodin's garden in the 7th to Monet's Water Lilies at the Orangerie, where a centenary show of almost forty Monet paintings runs until January. Sunday is a slow walk up the Canal Saint-Martin to the cliffs of the Buttes-Chaumont, then dinner under the Art Nouveau glass at Bouillon Julien.

Early November is short-day weather: dark by about 17:15, mild but showery, with every museum stop under a roof. Two things to plan around: Yellow Vests marches are called for Saturday, which usually means some central metro stations close for the afternoon, and metro line 6 is shut all Sunday. Armistice Day falls on Wednesday, November 11, after you've gone home.

days.title: Friday: the Marais and Île Saint-Louis
days.intro: Seventeenth-century squares and mansions turned museums, a falafel line worth joining, and a cocktail bar for the end of the night.

stops.name: Place des Vosges
stops.text: Start under the arcades of the oldest planned square in Paris, built under Henri IV, with brick and stone pavilions on all four sides and a garden of clipped lime trees in the middle. Walk the whole arcade loop before the shops open: galleries, a few cafés and, at number 28, the pavilion where the Pavillon de la Reine hotel now sits. The square is a five-minute walk from Carnavalet, so there's no need to hurry. Take a coffee and croissant at any café on the arcades; it's the view you're paying for.

stops.name: Musée Carnavalet
stops.text: The museum of the history of Paris fills two Marais mansions with the city's own story: shop signs, painted salons, revolutionary relics and recreated rooms, including Proust's bedroom. It's the best way to understand the streets you're about to walk. The permanent collection is free and you rarely need to book; temporary shows are paid and worth booking ahead. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, last entry 17:15, closed Mondays.

stops.name: L'As du Fallafel
stops.text: Friday lunch is the moment for the famous falafel window on rue des Rosiers, because it shuts early Friday afternoon and stays closed for Shabbat until Sunday. The pita is stuffed with "no fewer than six crispy falafel balls," as The Infatuation's Emily Monaco put it, plus cabbage, fried eggplant and tahini. The line moves fast and you pay while you wait. Eat it in Square Charles-Victor Langlois nearby, or join the shorter queue for a seat inside. Open Friday 11:00 to 17:00.

stops.name: Musée Picasso
stops.text: The Hôtel Salé holds the largest public collection of Picasso's work, and this autumn it shares the house with *Kurt Schwitters. Le chaos-monde 1918-1948*, a big show on the German collage artist that runs until February 7. A smaller room looks at Picasso and André Malraux's "imaginary museum." Allow two hours. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30 to 18:00; book a slot online to skip the ticket line.

stops.name: Île Saint-Louis and Berthillon
stops.text: Cross the Pont Marie onto the quieter of the two islands and walk its main street end to end, then loop back along the quays as the light goes; the view of Notre-Dame's restored roof from the island's western tip is the one to wait for. On the way, stop at Berthillon, the island's ice-cream maker since the 1950s. Even in November the salted-butter caramel and the seasonal marron glacé are worth a cone. Open Wednesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 20:00.

stops.name: Chez Janou
stops.text: A Provençal bistro a block from Place des Vosges, loud and warm on a Friday night, with a long pastis list behind the bar. Order the prawns flambéed in pastis or the duck breast with potatoes cooked in duck fat. It's open for lunch and dinner every day. Reserve, and arrive on time; tables don't wait.

stops.name: Little Red Door
stops.text: Behind a small red door on rue Charlot is a cocktail bar that has spent years on the world's best-bar lists, where the whole menu changes each season around a single idea. Order from the concept menu rather than the classics; that's where the work goes. Open daily 18:30 to 02:00. Bar seats are first come; call to reserve a table if you're a group.

days.title: Saturday: Rodin, Monet and a free night of photographs
days.intro: From the 7th arrondissement across the Seine to the Tuileries and Les Halles, with sculpture in the morning and pictures until 21:00.

stops.name: Coutume Café
stops.text: A roastery café on a quiet street behind Le Bon Marché, and one of the places that changed coffee in Paris. Order a filter coffee, brewed as V60 or Chemex, and something from the brunch menu if you want a proper breakfast before the museums. Bags of the house beans make a good thing to carry home. Open weekends 9:00 to 18:00.

stops.name: Musée Rodin
stops.text: Rodin's last studio, the Hôtel Biron, holds *The Kiss*, the room of Camille Claudel's sculptures and thousands of his drawings, while *The Thinker*, *The Gates of Hell* and *The Burghers of Calais* stand in the garden under the Invalides dome. Go early, before the garden fills, and do the garden first if it's dry. Full price is €13, free for under-26s. Open Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00.

stops.name: L'Ami Jean
stops.text: Stéphane Jégo's Basque-leaning bistro near the Invalides is cramped, loud and generous, and Saturday lunch is easier than dinner. Gault&Millau singles out the terrine and the haddock with celery and meat jus; the menu ends with the house rice pudding, which regulars come back for. Open Tuesday to Saturday, lunch from 12:00. Book online.

stops.name: Monet, Painting Time at the Orangerie
stops.text: Walk across the Pont de la Concorde to the Orangerie, home of Monet's oval rooms of *Water Lilies*. For the centenary of his death the museum has added almost forty more Monet paintings, from the Impressionist years to the series of haystacks, poplars and Rouen Cathedral, most lent by the Orsay and the Marmottan. A timed ticket is €12.50. Open daily except Tuesday, 9:00 to 18:00.

stops.name: Bourse de Commerce: free late opening
stops.text: On the first Saturday of each month the Pinault Collection opens Tadao Ando's concrete drum inside the old grain exchange for free from about 17:00 to 21:00. This month that means *Remember Me*, around 700 photographs by Irving Penn, Cindy Sherman, Man Ray, Cartier-Bresson, Avedon and more, with Barbara Kruger's text installation filling the rotunda. Free tickets go fast; reserve on the Pinault Collection site as soon as you can.

stops.name: Au Pied de Cochon
stops.text: Two minutes from the Bourse, this brasserie has fed the Les Halles neighbourhood since 1947, when the city's food market still stood across the road. Order the namesake stuffed pig's trotter with gribiche sauce, or play safe with oysters and a cassoulet. It serves from early morning until about 5:00, so there's no rush after the museum. On a march day, check which metro stations are open before you head home.

days.title: Sunday: Canal Saint-Martin and the Buttes-Chaumont
days.intro: A late brunch, a walk up the canal and into a park built on old quarries, an hour under the sea, and dinner in a 1906 dining room.

stops.name: Holybelly
stops.text: The café that taught Paris to queue for pancakes. Order the savoury stack, two pancakes with fried eggs, maple bacon and bourbon butter, a house signature since 2013, with a drip coffee. There are no reservations, and weekend waits run 30 to 45 minutes from 10:30, so get there at opening if you hate lines. Open daily 9:00 to 17:00, last food order 16:00.

stops.name: Canal Saint-Martin
stops.text: Walk north along the Quai de Valmy and the Quai de Jemmapes, crossing the iron footbridges and watching the locks fill if a boat is coming through. Keep going past the Rotonde de la Villette to the Bassin de la Villette, the wide basin where the canal opens out. It's about 40 minutes at an easy pace. If it's raining, cut across to the park by metro line 7 bis.

stops.name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
stops.text: Napoleon III's engineers turned old gypsum quarries into the city's most dramatic park in the 1860s: a lake, a cliff-top temple modelled on the Sibyl's temple at Tivoli, a suspension bridge and steep paths with long views east over the rooftops. Climb to the temple first, then wander down. Bring a coffee from the kiosks by the gates; in November the views beat anything you'll find in a café.

stops.name: Planète Océan at the Atelier des Lumières
stops.text: A former foundry where the walls and floor become one 360-degree screen. The current show is a 50-minute documentary dive from plankton to whales and polar ice, narrated in French with French and English subtitles. It's a good wet-afternoon plan, and children like it. Tickets are €18 full price and €11 for children; book a slot through Fever from the official site, and check Sunday times when you do.

stops.name: Bouillon Julien
stops.text: Finish in one of the most beautiful dining rooms in Paris, opened in 1906: Louis Trézel's four stained-glass women of the seasons, a mosaic floor and a mahogany bar by Louis Majorelle. The menu is the bouillon tradition: French classics at low prices, served fast. It's open every day from late morning to midnight, and no reservation is needed; on a Sunday night the wait is usually short.

stay.name: Le Pavillon de la Reine
stay.text: Set back behind a garden courtyard on Place des Vosges, where Anne of Austria is said to have stayed before her marriage to Louis XIII. Beamed rooms, duplex suites over the square and a 250-square-metre spa with a hammam and jacuzzi make it the place to come back to after a wet Friday. Everything on Friday's plan is a walk away.

stay.name: Hôtel du Petit Moulin
stay.text: Seventeen rooms in what was once the oldest bakery in Paris, with its painted shopfront kept intact and each room decorated differently by Christian Lacroix. It's a four-star with real character, on rue de Poitou in the Haut-Marais, a few doors from Little Red Door and a short walk to Picasso and Carnavalet.

stay.name: Hôtel Providence
stay.text: A small boutique hotel on rue René Boulanger, near Strasbourg-Saint-Denis, that suits Sunday's plan: Holybelly, the canal and Bouillon Julien are all within a short walk. The restaurant downstairs serves a Sunday brunch from 11:00 to 15:00. Rooms are compact, and prices are well below the Marais.

events.name: Louvre Photo
events.when: Opened Nov. 4; daily except Tue., through May 3, 2027
events.text: More than 300 photographs of the Louvre itself, from the invention of photography to new commissions by Robert Polidori and others: its artworks, galleries, visitors, staff and back rooms. Part of France's photography bicentenary; curated by Quentin Bajac and Dominique de Font-Réaulx.

events.name: PhotoSaintGermain
events.text: The 15th edition of the Left Bank photography festival, free, in galleries, schools, bookshops, hotels and institutions. Highlights include Guillaume Herbaut at the Académie des beaux-arts, Karen Knorr at the Musée Eugène-Delacroix and Tina Barney at Zander Galerie.

events.name: Bourse de Commerce free late opening
events.where: Bourse de Commerce, 2 Rue de Viarmes, 1st
events.text: The monthly free evening at the Pinault Collection, this time with *Remember Me*, its first exhibition given entirely to photography (normally €15). Free tickets must be reserved and go quickly.

events.name: Family dance weekend at the Musée Picasso
events.text: "Dansez maintenant !": flamenco, hip-hop and voguing classes, performances and workshops for all ages, free with museum admission.

events.name: PSG v Troyes
events.text: Ligue 1 matchweek 10 for the champions at home. Expect crowded trains on metro lines 9 and 10 before and after the game.

events.name: Rolex Paris Masters final
events.when: Sun. doubles 12:30 p.m., singles not before 3 p.m.
events.where: Paris La Défense Arena (now Plénitude Arena), Nanterre
events.text: The last ATP Masters 1000 of the season ends on Sunday, with Saturday's semifinal session from 11:30 a.m. Reach the arena by RER A or metro line 1 to La Défense.

know: **From CDG:** RER B runs to Gare du Nord and Châtelet–Les Halles on the €14 airport ticket. On Friday, November 6, from 22:45 there are no trains between Châtelet and the airport, with replacement buses, so late Friday arrivals should take a bus or a taxi. The airport branch runs normally at the weekend, though the line is cut between Aulnay and Mitry-Claye on the other branch. Official taxi flat fares were €56 to the Right Bank and €65 to the Left Bank last week.

**From Orly:** Metro line 14 runs from Orly to Châtelet, Pyramides and Saint-Lazare on the same airport ticket, and is the easy way in. RER C is suspended on several sections, including Austerlitz–Orly via Pont de Rungis, on Friday evening from 21:07 to 23:00.

**Tickets and closures:** A single metro ticket is €2.55, loaded onto a Navigo Easy card at any station machine. Saint-Michel on line 4 and République on line 8 are closed. **Metro line 6 is closed all day Sunday, November 8,** between Charles de Gaulle–Étoile and La Motte-Picquet–Grenelle, with replacement buses; this plan doesn't need it.

**Protests:** The Yellow Vests have called for blockades on Friday and a fourth national day of marches ("Act IV") on Saturday, November 7. No Paris route had been announced by November 2. On recent Saturdays 25 to 40 metro and RER stations closed during marches, and a night curfew covered République and Les Halles on October 31 to November 2; none has been announced for this weekend. Check the RATP app and the Police Prefecture before Saturday's evening at Les Halles.
**Strikes:** The national inter-union and SNCF strike is on Thursday, November 5; no strike is called for Friday to Sunday, but check trains if you arrive on Thursday.

**Museum days:** Carnavalet, Picasso and Rodin close on Mondays, the Orangerie and the Louvre on Tuesdays. Wednesday, November 11, Armistice Day, is a public holiday. Paris Photo runs at the Grand Palais from November 12 to 15, the week after this one.
**Tipping:** Service is included in French bills by law. Rounding up for coffee or leaving a few euros after a good dinner is a courtesy, not an obligation.
**Weather and light:** The forecast is mild but unsettled, with showers, and it's dark by about 17:15. Every afternoon in this plan has an indoor option.
